title: Probability Adventure 1: The Basics
welcome_lead: Welcome to probability! You'll learn the 0-to-1 scale, calculate P(event), and meet mutually exclusive events.
meta_desc: GCSE Maths Probability — the 0-to-1 scale, P(event) = favourable/total, fair dice and coins, mutually exclusive events.

concepts.def: Chance of an event happening, between 0 and 1
An outcome or set of outcomes you care about
Each outcome is equally likely to happen
Favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes
Events that cannot both happen at the same time

walkthroughs.body_html:
All probabilities live between 0 and 1.

  • 0 = impossible (e.g. rolling a 7 on a normal dice)
  • 1 = certain (e.g. the sun rising)
  • 0.5 = even chance (e.g. a fair coin landing on heads)

You can write probabilities as fractions, decimals or percentages.

For a fair situation:

P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes

Example: a fair six-sided dice. P(rolling a 4) = 1/6. P(rolling an even number) = 3/6 = 1/2, because there are 3 even outcomes (2, 4, 6) out of 6.

Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together — like "rolling a 2" and "rolling a 5" on one dice.

If you list all possible mutually exclusive outcomes, their probabilities add to 1.

P(A) + P(B) + ... = 1

So if P(red) = 0.3 and P(blue) = 0.2, then P(any other colour) = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5.

mcqs.q: What is the probability of an IMPOSSIBLE event?
Two events are mutually exclusive if...
options: They cannot happen at the same time

numericals.q: A fair six-sided dice is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a number GREATER than 4? Give your answer as a decimal.
numericals.hint: Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6 — that's 2 out of 6.

free_texts.q: P(red) = 0.4 and P(blue) = 0.35 in a bag with only red, blue and green counters. What is P(green)? Decimal only.
